# Chapter 5 Practice: Gases

*Auto-generated from the assessment guide (`assessment-support/gases.md`), grouped by objective. 26 questions spanning multiple-choice, short-answer, and workout formats. Within each objective the questions run from easier to harder.*

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 1
{{sp[info] Objective 5.1a}} · *multiple-choice* Which of the following is **not** a general characteristic of gases?

A. They take the shape and volume of their container
B. They are highly compressible
C. They have densities comparable to liquids
D. They mix evenly and completely with one another
:::
::: tab Answer
**C.** Gases are roughly a thousand times less dense than liquids, because the same molecules are spread over a far larger volume.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 2
{{sp[info] Objective 5.1a}} · *workout* Convert 725 mmHg to atm and to kPa.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$725\,\text{mmHg}\times\frac{1\,\text{atm}}{760\,\text{mmHg}}=0.954\ \text{atm}$$
$$725\,\text{mmHg}\times\frac{101325\,\text{Pa}}{760\,\text{mmHg}}\times\frac{1\,\text{kPa}}{1000\,\text{Pa}}=96.7\ \text{kPa}$$

Check: 725 is just below 760, so the answer in atm must be just below 1. ✓
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 3
{{sp[info] Objective 5.1a}} · *workout* A pressure gauge reads $3.50\times10^4$ Pa. Express this in atm and in torr.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$3.50\times10^4\,\text{Pa}\times\frac{1\,\text{atm}}{101325\,\text{Pa}}=0.345\ \text{atm}$$
$$3.50\times10^4\,\text{Pa}\times\frac{760\,\text{torr}}{101325\,\text{Pa}}=263\ \text{torr}$$

This runs the opposite way from Q2, so every conversion factor is inverted. Decide which unit must cancel before writing anything down.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 4
{{sp[info] Objective 5.1a}} · *short answer* Explain why a mercury barometer at sea level supports a column about 760 mm high, and predict what happens to that height at the top of a mountain.
:::
::: tab Answer
The atmosphere presses down on the exposed mercury surface in the dish, pushing mercury up the evacuated tube until the weight of the raised column exactly balances that push. At sea level the balance point is about 760 mm, which is why 760 mmHg was defined as 1 atm.

On a mountain there is less atmosphere above you, so the downward push is smaller and the column it can support is **shorter**. Barometric altimeters work on exactly this principle.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 5
{{sp[info] Objective 5.2a}} · *workout* What volume is occupied by 2.50 mol of an ideal gas at 1.00 atm and 25.0 °C?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$V=\frac{nRT}{P}=\frac{2.50\,\text{mol}\times0.0821\times298.15\,\text{K}}{1.00\,\text{atm}}=61.2\ \text{L}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 6
{{sp[info] Objective 5.2a}} · *workout* A 5.00 L cylinder holds 0.750 mol of gas at 15.0 atm. What is the temperature in °C?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$T=\frac{PV}{nR}=\frac{15.0\,\text{atm}\times5.00\,\text{L}}{0.750\,\text{mol}\times0.0821}=1218\ \text{K}$$

Convert back to Celsius as the question asks: $1218-273=945\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

The equation always works in kelvin; converting is the last step, never the first.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 7
{{sp[info] Objective 5.2a}} · *workout* A balloon holds 4.00 L at 25.0 °C and 1.00 atm. It is cooled to −10.0 °C at constant pressure. What is its new volume?
:::
::: tab Answer
The amount of gas and the pressure are both unchanged, so the combined law reduces to $V_i/T_i = V_f/T_f$.

$$V_f=V_i\times\frac{T_f}{T_i}=4.00\,\text{L}\times\frac{263.15\,\text{K}}{298.15\,\text{K}}=3.53\ \text{L}$$

{{sp[warning] Watch out}} Using Celsius would give $4.00\times(-10.0/25.0)=-1.6$ L — a negative volume, which is a useful sign that something went wrong. Ratios of temperature require an absolute scale.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 8
{{sp[info] Objective 5.2a}} · *workout* A weather balloon holds 25.0 L at 1.00 atm and 20.0 °C at ground level. At altitude the pressure is 0.350 atm and the temperature −35.0 °C. What is its volume there?
:::
::: tab Answer
Both pressure and temperature change, so use the full combined law.

$$V_f=V_i\times\frac{P_i}{P_f}\times\frac{T_f}{T_i}=25.0\,\text{L}\times\frac{1.00}{0.350}\times\frac{238.15\,\text{K}}{293.15\,\text{K}}=58.0\ \text{L}$$

The two effects oppose each other: the pressure drop alone would nearly triple the volume, while the cooling shrinks it by about 19%. The pressure effect wins, which is why weather balloons expand as they rise and eventually burst.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 9
{{sp[info] Objective 5.2b}} · *workout* What is the density of $\ce{O2}$ (32.00 g/mol) at 1.00 atm and 25.0 °C?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$d=\frac{P\mathcal{M}}{RT}=\frac{1.00\,\text{atm}\times32.00\,\text{g/mol}}{0.0821\times298.15\,\text{K}}=1.31\ \text{g/L}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 10
{{sp[info] Objective 5.2b}} · *workout* A gas has a density of 1.34 g/L at 1.00 atm and 0.0 °C. What is its molar mass, and what gas might it be?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$\mathcal{M}=\frac{dRT}{P}=\frac{1.34\,\text{g/L}\times0.0821\times273.15\,\text{K}}{1.00\,\text{atm}}=30.0\ \text{g/mol}$$

Since these are STP conditions you could equally multiply by the molar volume: $1.34\ \text{g/L}\times22.41\ \text{L/mol}=30.0$ g/mol. ✓

30.0 g/mol is consistent with **nitrogen monoxide, $\ce{NO}$** (30.01 g/mol) or with ethane, $\ce{C2H6}$ (30.07). Molar mass alone cannot distinguish them — it never can.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 11
{{sp[info] Objective 5.2b}} · *workout* For $\ce{2KClO3(s) -> 2KCl(s) + 3O2(g)}$, what volume of $\ce{O2}$ is produced from 12.0 g of $\ce{KClO3}$ (122.55 g/mol) at 25.0 °C and 1.00 atm?
:::
::: tab Answer
**Steps 1 and 2 — to moles of the gas**, exactly as in Chapter 3:

$$12.0\,\text{g}\times\frac{1\,\text{mol}\,\ce{KClO3}}{122.55\,\text{g}}\times\frac{3\,\text{mol}\,\ce{O2}}{2\,\text{mol}\,\ce{KClO3}}=0.1469\ \text{mol}\,\ce{O2}$$

**Step 3 — moles to volume:**

$$V=\frac{nRT}{P}=\frac{0.1469\times0.0821\times298.15}{1.00}=3.59\ \text{L}$$

The conditions are not STP, so 22.41 L/mol does not apply here.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 12
{{sp[info] Objective 5.3a}} · *workout* A container holds 0.300 mol $\ce{N2}$ and 0.200 mol $\ce{O2}$ at a total pressure of 2.00 atm. Find the mole fraction and partial pressure of each.
:::
::: tab Answer
Total moles: $0.300+0.200=0.500$ mol.

$$X_{\ce{N2}}=\frac{0.300}{0.500}=0.600 \qquad X_{\ce{O2}}=\frac{0.200}{0.500}=0.400$$
$$P_{\ce{N2}}=0.600\times2.00=1.20\ \text{atm} \qquad P_{\ce{O2}}=0.400\times2.00=0.800\ \text{atm}$$

**Checks:** mole fractions sum to 1.000, and partial pressures sum to 2.00 atm. ✓
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 13
{{sp[info] Objective 5.3a}} · *short answer* Two 1.0 L flasks at the same temperature each hold 0.10 mol of gas — one helium, one xenon. Compare their pressures.
:::
::: tab Answer
**The pressures are identical.**

$PV=nRT$ contains no term for the identity of the gas. Equal moles in equal volumes at equal temperature give equal pressure, whether the molecules are light or heavy.

The xenon atoms move much more slowly, but each carries far more momentum, and the two effects cancel exactly. This is the same fact as Avogadro's law, and it is why a mole fraction determines a partial-pressure share regardless of which gas it is.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 14
{{sp[info] Objective 5.3a}} · *workout* A 2.00 L vessel at 27.0 °C contains 1.60 g $\ce{O2}$ (32.00 g/mol) and 0.28 g $\ce{N2}$ (28.02 g/mol). Find the partial pressure of each gas and the total pressure.
:::
::: tab Answer
Convert masses to moles first — the equation needs moles, not grams.

$$n_{\ce{O2}}=\frac{1.60}{32.00}=0.0500\ \text{mol}\qquad n_{\ce{N2}}=\frac{0.28}{28.02}=0.0100\ \text{mol}$$

Each gas exerts its own pressure in the full 2.00 L, at 300.15 K:

$$P_{\ce{O2}}=\frac{0.0500\times0.0821\times300.15}{2.00}=0.616\ \text{atm}$$
$$P_{\ce{N2}}=\frac{0.0100\times0.0821\times300.15}{2.00}=0.123\ \text{atm}$$
$$P_{\text{total}}=0.616+0.123=0.739\ \text{atm}$$

Note that each gas uses the *whole* volume, not a share of it — that is exactly what "as if the other were not there" means.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 15
{{sp[info] Objective 5.3b}} · *short answer* Why must a correction be applied when a gas is collected over water, and in which direction does forgetting it push your answer?
:::
::: tab Answer
Water evaporates into the collected gas until its vapor reaches the equilibrium pressure for that temperature, so the tube contains a **mixture**. The measured total pressure is the sum of the gas's partial pressure and the water vapor's.

Forgetting to subtract the water vapor pressure means attributing all the pressure to your gas, which **overstates** the moles collected. The error is always in that direction.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 16
{{sp[info] Objective 5.3b}} · *workout* 245 mL of $\ce{O2}$ is collected over water at 22.0 °C. The atmospheric pressure is 754 mmHg and the vapor pressure of water at 22.0 °C is 19.8 mmHg. How many moles of $\ce{O2}$ were collected?
:::
::: tab Answer
**Correct the pressure first:**
$$P_{\ce{O2}}=754-19.8=734\ \text{mmHg}=\frac{734}{760}=0.966\ \text{atm}$$

**Then apply the ideal gas equation** at 295.15 K:
$$n=\frac{PV}{RT}=\frac{0.966\times0.245}{0.0821\times295.15}=9.77\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 17
{{sp[info] Objective 5.3b}} · *workout* Using the result of Q16, what mass of $\ce{O2}$ (32.00 g/mol) was collected, and what mass would you have reported had you forgotten the water-vapor correction?
:::
::: tab Answer
**Correct answer:** $9.77\times10^{-3}\,\text{mol}\times32.00\,\text{g/mol}=0.312\ \text{g}$.

**Without the correction:** $P=754/760=0.992$ atm, giving $n=1.00\times10^{-2}$ mol and a mass of **0.321 g**.

The uncorrected value is 2.7% too high. In a titration or a yield calculation that is the difference between a clean result and an unexplained excess.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 18
{{sp[info] Objective 5.4a}} · *multiple-choice* According to the kinetic molecular theory, the average kinetic energy of gas molecules depends on

A. the molar mass of the gas
B. the pressure of the gas
C. the absolute temperature only
D. the volume of the container
:::
::: tab Answer
**C.** Assumption 4 states $\overline{KE}\propto T$ with no reference to the gas's identity. Two different gases at the same temperature have the same average kinetic energy — though not the same average speed, since the heavier one must move more slowly to match.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 19
{{sp[info] Objective 5.4a}} · *short answer* Use the kinetic molecular theory to explain why the pressure of a gas rises when it is compressed at constant temperature.
:::
::: tab Answer
Pressure is produced by molecules striking the container walls, and it depends on how often they strike.

Compressing the gas does not change how many molecules there are or how fast they move (temperature is constant), but it packs them into a smaller volume. The number of molecules per unit volume rises, so each molecule has a shorter distance to travel before reaching a wall, and the **collision rate rises**. More impacts per second on each unit of wall area means higher pressure.

This is Boyle's law, $P\propto1/V$, expressed as a mechanism rather than a graph.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 20
{{sp[info] Objective 5.4a}} · *workout* Calculate $u_{rms}$ for $\ce{CO2}$ (44.01 g/mol) at 300 K.
:::
::: tab Answer
Use $R=8.314$ J/(K·mol) and the molar mass **in kg/mol**:

$$u_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{\mathcal{M}}}=\sqrt{\frac{3\times8.314\times300}{0.04401}}=412\ \text{m/s}$$

Forgetting to convert g/mol to kg/mol is the standard error here; it would inflate the answer by a factor of $\sqrt{1000}\approx32$.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 21
{{sp[info] Objective 5.4b}} · *short answer* Distinguish diffusion from effusion.
:::
::: tab Answer
**Diffusion** is the gradual mixing of one gas through another by random molecular motion — a perfume spreading across a room.

**Effusion** is the escape of a gas through a small opening into a region of lower pressure or a vacuum — a helium balloon slowly deflating.

Both depend on how fast molecules move, so both follow Graham's law, but they are physically different processes: diffusion happens *within* a mixture, effusion happens *through a barrier*.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 22
{{sp[info] Objective 5.4b}} · *workout* How much faster does $\ce{H2}$ (2.016 g/mol) effuse than $\ce{O2}$ (32.00 g/mol)?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$\frac{r_{\ce{H2}}}{r_{\ce{O2}}}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathcal{M}_{\ce{O2}}}{\mathcal{M}_{\ce{H2}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{32.00}{2.016}}=\sqrt{15.87}=3.98$$

Hydrogen effuses about **4 times faster**. Sanity check the direction: the lighter gas must be faster, and the answer exceeds 1. ✓

Note that $\ce{O2}$ is nearly 16 times heavier but only 4 times slower — the square root cuts the effect in half on a logarithmic scale.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 23
{{sp[info] Objective 5.4b}} · *workout* It takes an unknown gas 4.50 times as long as helium (4.003 g/mol) to effuse through the same opening. What is its molar mass?
:::
::: tab Answer
Longer time means slower rate, and Graham's law relates the two directly: $t_2/t_1 = \sqrt{\mathcal{M}_2/\mathcal{M}_1}$.

$$\frac{t_{\text{unk}}}{t_{\ce{He}}}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathcal{M}_{\text{unk}}}{\mathcal{M}_{\ce{He}}}} \;\Longrightarrow\; 4.50=\sqrt{\frac{\mathcal{M}_{\text{unk}}}{4.003}}$$

$$\mathcal{M}_{\text{unk}}=4.003\times4.50^2=4.003\times20.25=81.1\ \text{g/mol}$$

Sanity check: it is slower than helium, so it must be heavier, and 81.1 > 4.003. ✓ Note that the time ratio and the rate ratio are reciprocals — read carefully which one the problem gives you.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 24
{{sp[info] Objective 5.5a}} · *multiple-choice* Real gases deviate most from ideal behavior at

A. high temperature and low pressure
B. low temperature and high pressure
C. high temperature and high pressure
D. standard temperature and pressure
:::
::: tab Answer
**B.** High pressure crowds the molecules so their own volume becomes significant; low temperature slows them so intermolecular attractions matter. These are also the conditions under which a gas is close to condensing.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 25
{{sp[info] Objective 5.5a}} · *short answer* Explain what each term in the van der Waals equation corrects, and what the equation becomes when both constants are zero.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$\left(P+\frac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V-nb)=nRT$$

The **$an^2/V^2$ term is added to the measured pressure**. Intermolecular attractions pull a molecule back as it approaches the wall, so it strikes with less force and the observed pressure is lower than ideal; adding this term restores it. A larger $a$ means stronger attractions.

The **$nb$ term is subtracted from the volume**. The molecules themselves occupy space, so the volume actually available for motion is less than the container's. A larger $b$ means larger molecules.

With $a=b=0$ the equation reduces to $PV=nRT$. The ideal gas equation is the special case where molecules have no size and no attractions.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 26
{{sp[info] Objective 5.5a}} · *short answer* Rank $\ce{He}$, $\ce{N2}$, and $\ce{H2O}$ vapor by how ideally you expect them to behave at 1 atm and 100 °C, and justify the ranking.
:::
::: tab Answer
**Most ideal: He > $\ce{N2}$ > $\ce{H2O}$ (least ideal).**

**Helium** is a small, nonpolar, monatomic gas with only the weakest attractions — both van der Waals corrections are tiny.

**Nitrogen** is slightly larger and still nonpolar, so its attractions are weak but not negligible.

**Water vapor** is strongly polar and forms hydrogen bonds (Chapter 11), so its molecules attract one another far more strongly than either of the others.

The ranking matches boiling points: helium boils at 4 K, nitrogen at 77 K, water at 373 K. Both facts measure the same underlying quantity — how strongly the molecules attract one another.
:::
::::
